ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Preservation of Tribal Culture in Orissa 
*481. SHRI MAN MOHAN SAMAL : Will the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state : 
(a) the various schemes being implemented by Gove rnment for the 
preservation of tribal culture in Orissa; and 
(b) whether Government propose to set up an institute for achieving the 
said purpose ? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JUAL ORAM): (a) The 
Ministry.of Tribal Affairs provides, financial assistance under Centrally 
Sponsored remain to Government of Orissa on match ing basis (50 : 50), as 
Grants in and to Tribal Resear ch and Training Institute, (TRI), 
Bhubaneshwar. One of the activities o f TRI is preservation of Tribal Culture. 
The Institute is engage in preparation of  tribal monographs of different tribal 
communities and it has got a museum with rich collection of various tribal 
artefacts. Besides, Department of Culture, Government of India, administers a 
scheme whereunder financial assistance is provided to voluntary organizations 
and individuals engaged in preservation  and promotion of tribal folk art and 
culture. 
In addition, Government of Orissa has also set up an Academy of Tribal 
Dialects and Culture, Bhubaneshwar. 
(b) No, Sir.

DR. M. N. DAS: Sir, at the outset, I should congratulate the hon. Minister 
for his excellent attention to preserve the tribal culture; specifically* I should 
congratulate him for his recent effort to establish a Department of Tribal Research 
and Studies in the newly-founded University of North Orissa, at Baripada, a 
central place for tribal culture. I was told by the Vice-Chancellor that they were 
going to study the origin and development of tribal alphabet, dialect, language, 
literature; they were also going to bring to the world notice what is tribal thought, 
tribal ways of living, tribal religion, faith and everything else. So, he deserves 
congratulation. 
At the same time, Sir, mere preservation of tribal culture is not enough; it is 
also important to preserve some of the tribal communities which are nearing 
extinction. I draw your attention to a small community of tribals known as 
Mankadia, in Simlipal Forest. They live on monkeys and monkeys are scared 
away from the forests. Can you take steps to bring that community out of the 
forest and give them some land to settle down near the Simlipal Hills ?

Secondary, it is an all-India question. Some 70 years ago, the famous 
German Anthropologist, Von Hemeindorff, came to discover some tribals who 
still maintained the traits of the Neo-lithic age like Juangs and they are almost on 
the verge of extinction. Some steps should be taken to preserve those special 
species still maintaining the trends of Neo-lithic age. Sir, finally, I request the 
hon. Minister to pay his attention to a very burning issue of tribal ways of 
cultivation. There is something called shifting cultivation. Every year tribals 
clear a part of the forest and plant thei r crops, and next year they shift their 
cultivation to the next place. The shif ting cultivation has caused an immense 
harm to the environment. It has led to deforestation. The soil of the hill comes 
down into the rivers and rivers change their courses, getting silted up. Therefore, 
something should be done to give them land outside the forests so that they can 
cultivate their field and maintain their livelihood.

Drugs for Athletes  
*486. SHRIRAJU PARMAR: SH RIBHAGATRAM MANHAR: Will 
the Minister ofHEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  a large number of drug stores/ 
chemists stock a number of performance enhancing drugs for athletes; 
(b) if so, the number of such cases which have been reported, so far; and 
(c) the action taken against the drug stores/chemists? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Under the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, drug 
stores and chemists are allowed to stock and undertake sale of only those drugs 
that are approved for manufacture and/or sale in the country. Drugs are 
approved for sale taking into account their quality, safety, efficacy and 
rationality. Some of the drugs including amphetamines, narcotic analgesics, 
anabolic steroids, stimulant drugs, diuretics etc., which are used for the treatment 
of various medical conditions are also reported to be used by sports persons to 
enhance their performance, although this practice is prohibited by national and 
international sporting bodies. Almost all these are listed in Schedule X and 
Schedule H of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945 and such drugs can only be 
purchased against prescription from Re gistered Medical Practitioners. Hence 
there are no specific drugs which are stocked by chemists and drug stores that 
fall under the category of performance enhancing drugs for athletes. 
No specific complaint has been received by the Drug Controller (India) 
about stocking and selling of any drug specifically for the purpose of enhancing 
the performance of sports persons. 
State Drug Controllers have been advised to keep a watch on the sale of 
such performance enhancing drugs, details of which have been obtained from 
the Sports Authority of India, and to report any violations noted regarding their 
sales without prescriptions.

Statement 
Provisions Relating to Assistance under the National Scheme of Liberation 
and Rehabilitation of Scavengers and their Dependents 
OBJECTIVES 
The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment has been operating the 
National Scheme of Liberation and Rehabilitation of Scavengers and their 
dependents (NSLRS). The objective of the scheme is to liberate scavengers from 
the hereditary and inhuman occupation of manually removing night soil and filth 
and to provide for and engage them in  alternative and dignified occupations. 
With this objective in view, the Government of India launched the Scheme in 
March, 1992, after splitting the erstwhile scheme of conversion of dry latrines 
and rehabilitation of liberated scavengers that was started in 1981-82. 
The main components of the scheme are :— 
(i)  Survey—Time bound programme for identification of scavengers 
and their dependents and their aptitude for alternative trade through 
a survey. 
(ii)   Training—The Scheme provides for training of scavengers in the 
age group of 15-50 years in the training institutes of Central 
Government, State Governments, Local Bodies and Non-
Governmental Organisations on TRYSEM norms. The training 
period should be for a maximum duration of 6 months. The stipend 
provided to a scavenger for training is upto Rs. 500/- per month. 
Besides this, the training fees per scavenger is upto Rs. 300/- per 
month, honorarium to craftsman upto Rs. 100 per month and toolkit 
allowance upto Rs. 2000/- per scavenger, is also permissible. The 
full cost of training is borne by Government of India. 
(iii) Rehabilitation—Towards rehabilitation of scavengers, projects 
costing upto Rs. 50,000/- for each beneficiary are financed by way 
of a prescribed financial package comprising of 50% subsidy subject 
to a ceiling of Rs. 10,000/- per project, 15% of project cost as Margin 
Money Loan (MML) which is shared between the Central 
Government and State Governments in the ratio 49 : 51 and the rest 
through bank loan.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) While some of the Honourable Members urged not to disinvest 
Government equity m Air India and to infuse fluids for revival of the Company, 
some Members expressed concern over the following issues relating to the 
disinvestment of Air India :— 
 Proper valuation of the Company 
 National interest and security concerns 
 Protection of employees' interest 
 Possibility of receiving single bjd offer from Tata-Singapore Airlines 
 Transparency in the bidding process 
Such letters have been replied to cl arifying the following stand of the 
Government in these matters : 
 Since infusion of huge funds for revival of Air India was not found 
advisable looking at the tact that large infusion of funds had not 
turned around, public sector companies, the decision to disinvest 
Government equity in Air India was taken after considering all aspects. 
 The Government, in consultation with various organizations, has put 
in place standardized nationa lly and internationally accepted 
valuation methodologies. In the case of Air India (AI), apart from 
42 

[27 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
the valuation to be done by th e Advisors in accordance with the 
approved methodologies, it has been decided that two other reputed 
valuers will also be asked to carry out an independent valuation of 
the Company in order to have utmost objectivity and transparency 
in making fair assessment of the value of the Company. 
     Provisions have been made in the shareholders agreement to take 
care of all the issues/concerns relating to national interest and 
security as well as for protection of employees' interest. 
      It   is not uncommon under standard Government procedures to 
 accept single bid offers provided  the bidding process was duly 
 advertised and the offer received is f ound to be competitive. In       
the case of Air India, the Government had properly advertised 
the disinvestment and undertook the process in a transparent and 
exhaustive manner. To ensure the competitiveness (even in the 
likelihood of a single bid offer), the reserve price of the Government 
would be determined through an objective valuation process. 
(c) The process of disinvestment of Air India has been undertaken in a 
systematic and totally transparent manner. The following procedure adopted for 
disinvestment of CPSUs applies to Air India as well: 
     Proposals for disinvestment in any PSU, based on the 
recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission or in accordance 
with the declared Disinvestment Policy of the Government, are placed 
for consideration of the Cabinet Committee on Disinvestment (CCD). 
     After CCD clears the disinvestment proposal, selection of the 
Advisors for assisting in the implementation of the disinvestment 
decision, is done through a competitive bidding process. 
    The Advisors assist the Government in preparation and issue of 
advertisement in leading newspapers/magazines/journals, for 
inviting Expression of Interest (Eol) from prospective Strategic 
Partners. In cases of urgency, Eol is prepared by Department of 
Disinvestment and issued after approval of Inter Ministerial Group 
(IMG). 
    After receipt of the Eol, Pr ospective Bidders are short listed, 
based on objective screening in the light of the announced pre-
qualification criteria/requirements. 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [27 August, 2001 ] 
 The Advisors, after due diligence of the PSU, prepare the Information 
Memorandum in consultation with the concerned PSU. This is given to 
the short listed Prospective Bidders, who have entered into a 
Confidentiality Agreement. 
 The draft Share Purchase Agreement or the Shareholders Agreement 
are also prepared by the Adviso rs, with the help of the Legal 
Advisors, and given to the Prospective Bidders for eliciting their 
reaction. 
 The Prospective Bidders undertake due diligence of the PSU and 
hold discussions with the Advisors/the Government/the 
representatives of the PSU for any clarifications. 
 Concurrently, the task of valuation of the PSU is undertaken in 
accordance with the standard national and international practices. In 
the specific case of Air India, the Business Valuation shall be done by 
three independent valuers. 
 Based on the reactions received from the Prospective Bidders, the 
Share Purchase Agreement and Shareholders Agreement are finalised and 
after vetting by the Ministry of Law, they are approved by the 
Government. Thereafter, they are sent to the Prospective Bidders for 
inviting the final binding bids (Technical and Financial). 
 After examination, analysis and evaluation of the bids, the 
recommendations of the Inter Ministerial Group (IMG) are placed 
before the CCD for a final decision regarding selection of the Strategic 
Partner, signing of the Share Purchase and Shareholders 
Agreements and other ancillary issues. 
 In the disinvestment process mentioned above. Department of 
Disinvestment is assisted at each stage by an Inter Ministerial Group 
(IMG) comprising officers from the Ministry of Finance, Department of 
Public Enterprises, the Administrative Ministry/Department 
controlling the PSU, the PSU concerned apart from the officers of the 
Department of Disinvestment and the Advisors. 
 After the transaction is completed, all papers and documents relating 
to it shall be turned over the Comptroller and Auditor General of India; 
the CAG shall prepare an evaluation for sending to Parliament and 
releasing to the public.

3680. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: 
            PROF. A. LAKSHMISAGAR : 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government are aware of the continuous manufacturing and 
marketing of spurious drugs in the country; 
(b) if so, whether any study has been made by Government to assess the 
situation and to identify the manufacturer s of the sub-standa rd drugs and the 
modus operandi of marketing their products; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the action taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRJ A. RAJA): (a) Yes, Sir. Government are aware of the 
problem of the manufacture, sale and distribution of spurious drugs, this is a 
clandestine activity indulged in by some unscrupulous and anti-social persons. 
60 

[27 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) to (d) No specific study has been made by Government in this regard. 
However, the Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare has constituted a 
Committee under the Chairmanship of DGHS on July 18,2001 associating members 
from Industry, Trade, Drugs Regulatory Officials and Public representatives to 
go into all aspects of the menace of Spurious drugs and suggest remedial 
measures. 
Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules 
thereunder, State Governments have been empowered to enforce quality of drugs 
including check on manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The said Act was 
amended in 1982 to provide for specific definition of spurious drugs and severe 
penalties extending to life imprisonment have been prescribed. 
State Governments have been advised from time to time to provide adequate 
enforcement machinery and drug testing facilities and to keep strict surveillance 
over the inter-state movement of spurious drugs. Facilities of Central Government 
testing labs have also been made available to the States for testing of drugs 
besides financial assistance provided to them to augment and strengthen their 
testing capabilities. 
The State Drugs Controllers have been advised to take the following 
measures for curbing the incidence of spurious drugs:- 
(i) Constitution/reactivation of Stat e Drug Advisory Committees in 
which various trade and industry association as well as consumer 
association should find representation. 
00 Establishment of separate intelligence-cum-legal machinery with 
police assistance. 
(iii) Training to be provided to selected Officials of Drug Control 
Administration in the modalities of intelligence work, prosecution 
etc, in respect of Spurious/Counterfeit drugs. 
(iv) To ensure speedy analysis of drugs samples by establishing own 
state level drug testing facilities. 
(v) State Drugs Control Authorities to be cautious while approving 
licences for drug products to ensure that "look alike" products are 
not encouraged. 
(vi) To develop efficient communication facilities and recall procedures. 
(vii) To undertake surveillance of suspected dealers. 
(viii) To engage experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug cases. 
61 

RAJYA SABHA [27 August, 2001 ] 
(be) To obtain Cooperation of Pharmaceutical Industry by regular 
interaction with them. 
(x) To collect survey samples under National Survey Quality Evaluation 
of Drug (NSQED) programme. 
Association of Pharmaceutical Indust ry and All India Organisation of 
Chemists and Druggists have been asked to take necessary initiative to 
collectively combat the menace of spurious drugs. 
The problem of manufacture and sale of spurious drugs and the need to 
ensure its checking has been specifically  explained to State Health Ministers 
during the meeting of Central Council of Health & Family Welfare.

 Action points identified during First Business Session ofEAG held on

The EAG resolved to work with the participating State in formulating their

of Medicine practitioners, integration of vertical societies of State 
and district levels, regular release of funds to operational levels, 
joint planning/training for the field staff of the cognate departments,

Revised National TB Control Programme 
3693. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM : Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in March, 2001 his Ministry has announced that the Revised 
National TB Control Programme would cover 400 million people in the country 
by the end of the year; 
(b) if so, the progress made, so far; 
(c) the salient features of the Revised TB Control Programme; 
(d) the number of people affected ever y year for the last five years, 
State-wise; and % 
75 

RAJYA SABHA [27 August, 2001 ] 
(e) the steps taken by Government to spread awareness in this respect? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 400 million population 
has already been covered under Revised National TB Control programme 
(RNTCP). 
(c) The objective of the Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) 
is to achieve a cure rate of at least 85% of new sputum positive cases and to 
detect at least 70% of such cases. Th e RNTCP is an application of the WHO 
recommended Directory Observed Treatment, Short course (DOTS) strategy to 
control TB. The components of the strategy are: (i) Political and administrative 
commitment at all levels, (ii) Diagnosis through quality sputum microscopy of 
patients attending peripheral health facilities, (iii) Uninterrupted supply of Short- 
Course Chemotherapy drugs, which are given in patient-wise boxes, (iv) Direct 
observation of treatment through involvement of peripheral health functionaries, 
NGOs and community volunteers, and (v) systematic monitoring, evaluation 
and supervision at all levels. 
Under the revised strategy, a success rate of more than 80% has been 
reported by the Project Districts which means that 8 out of 10 TB patients put on 
treatment under the revised strategy ar e successfully treated as against less 
than 4 out of 10 under the previous programme. 
(d) Under the National TB Control Programme, about 14 lakhs TB cases 
are detected and put on treatment in the country every year. Approximately 40% 
TB cases report to private sector for treatment. Thus it is estimated that about 22       
lakhs new TB cases are occurring in the country every year. A statement 
indicating the State-wise details of TB cases detected and put under treatment 
under the National TB Control Programme during the last 5 years is annexed.         
(See below) 
(e) For creating awareness in general public information about signs and 
symptoms of TB and availability of its diagnostic and treatment facilities, is 
disseminated through publication of DO's and DON'T's in newspapers. The IEC 
activities have been decentralized under the Programme and they are being 
undertaken by the District TB Societies through the Central assistance given for 
the purpose to them.

Review of population growth 
3694. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD : Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government have reviewed the progress made, so far, in 
controlling population growth vis-a-vis the huge expenditure incurred every year on 
family planning in the country; 
(b) if so, the outcome thereof; 
(c) whether any concrete measures including effective incentives have been or 
proposed to be adopted for curbing population rise; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) Review of the National Family Welfare 
Programme including budget requirement of each activities is being carried out 
periodically. 
The progress in reducing population growth rate does not depend only on 
expenditure incurred on family planning but also many other socio-economic factors, such 
as success in increasing literacy, particularly of women, age at marriage, improvement 
in infrastructure, sanitation, transport, communication in addition to improving 
reproductive health services. 
However, the changes that have taken .place since inception of National Family 
Welfare Programme in key indicators are given in the Statement. (See below). 
78 

[27 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) and (d) The National Population Policy, 2000 adopted by the 
Government of India in February, 2000 affirms the commitment of the Government 
towards voluntary and informed choice and consent of citizens while availing 
themselves of reproductive health care services. The policy enumerates certain 
notional socio-demographic goals to be achieved by 2010, which are expected to 
stabilize the population in the country by 2045. 
The Policy also provides for certain promotional and motivational measures 
which are listed below: 
1.   Panchayats and Zila Parishads will be rewarded and honoured for 
exemplary performance in universalising the small family norm, 
achieving reductions in infant mortality and birth rates, and promoting 
literacy with completion of primary schooling. 
2 .   The Balika Samridhi Yojana run by the Department of Women 
and Child Development, to promote survival and care of the girl 
child, will continue. A cash inceniive of Rs. 500 is awarded at the 
birth of the girl child of birth order 1 or 2. 
3. The Maternity Benefit Scheme newly operated by Department of 
Family Welfare provides a cash grant of Rs. 500 to mothers who 
have their first child after 19 years of age, for birth of the first or 
second child only. 
4. A Family Welfare-linked health Insurance Plan will be established. 
Couples below the poverty line, who undergo sterilisation, With not 
more than two living children, would become eligible (alone with 
children) for health insurance (for hospitalisation) not exceeding 
Rs. 5000, and a personal accident insurance cover for the spouse 
undergoing sterilisation. 
5. Couples below the poverty line, who marry after the legal age of 
marriage, register the marriage, have their first child after the mother 
reaches the age of 21, accept the small family norm, and adopt a 
terminal method after birth of the second child, will be rewarded. 
6. A revolving fund will be set up for income-generating activities by 
village-level self help groups, who provide community-level health 
care services. 
7. Creches and childcare centres will be opened in rural areas and 
urban slums. This will facilitate and promote participation of women 
in paid employment. 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [27 August, 2001 ] 
8. A wider, affordable choice of contraceptives will be made accessible 
at diverse delivery points, with counselling services to enable 
acceptors to exercise voluntary and informed consent. 
9. Facilities for safe abortion will be strengthened and expanded. 
 
10. Products and services will be made affordable through innovative 
social marketing schemes. 
11. Local entrepreneurs at village levels will be provided soft loans arid 
encouraged to run ambulance services to supplement the existing 
arrangements for referral transportation. 
12. Increased vocational training schemes for girls, leading to self-
employment will be encouraged. 
13. Strict enforcement of Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1976 will be 
ensured. 
14. Strict enforcement of the Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994 
will be ensured. 
15. Soft loans to ensure mobility of the ANMs will be increased. 
16. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment has frozen the number of 
representatives in the Lok Sabha (on the basis of population) at 
1971 Census levels. The freeze is currently valid until 2001, and has 
served as an incentive for State Governments to fearlessly pursue 
the agenda for popula tion stabilization. The freeze needs to be 
extended until 2026.

Improvement in Mental Health Care  
3695. SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN : Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any steps to improve the 'mental 
health care' after the incident at 'Ervadi' in Tamil Nadu; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to help the victims of the Ervadi 
incident? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) Government of Tamil Nadu 
have initiated actions for prevention of such incidents in the future. A psychiatrist 
has been posted to Ervadi Primary Health Centre with adequate supply of 
psychiatric medicines and Health Inspector had been instructed to visit places 
where mentally ill are detained. Government of Tamil Nadu has decided to permit 
only licensed premises for such mentally ill persons and shut down all unlicensed 
premises. Heads of Department of Psychiatry of all Government Medical Colleges 
have been appointed as Inspecting Officers for inspection of Psychiatric Hospital/ 
Nursing Homes. Steps have been taken to send the patient who have shown 
substantial improvement to their families and other patients to Mental Health 
Institutions run by the Government. A Monitoring Committee is being set up in 
each district under the chairmanship of the District Collector, Psychiatrist and 
district health authorities to monitor all such institutions to ensure the guidelines 
to be formulated by the State Mental  Health Authority are followed and a 
Psychiatrist will be posted to all the District Headquarters Hospitals for better 
mental health care. All District Collectors have been directed to make immediate 
inspection of all shelters for mentally ill and ensure that in future no such shelter 
is allowed to function without getting a license as per Mental Health Act, 1987. 
(c) The Government of Tamil Nadu hadjgranted Rs. 15,000/- to the relatives 
of each deceased. Out of 571 mentally ill patients released from the shelters in 
and around Ervadi, 273 patients had been taken back by the relatives, 20 patients 
had been admitted in Ramanathapuram Government Hospital and the remaining 
278 patients are being examined by a team of psychiatrists. The 200 chronically 
ill patients will be admitted to the Institute of Mental Health, Chennai for 
treatment and the remaining persons will be rehabilitated by the Collector 
Ramanathapuram in consultation with District Health Officials.

proportions; 
(b) if so, the extent of the problem of different types of heart diseases in 
the country; 
(c) the various reasons therefor and the age-group most affected; and % 
(d) the measures being taken or proposed to be taken to control the 
diseases? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) According to Indian 
Council of Medical Research, Cardiovascular Diseases (CVD) are major 
contributor to  mortality and morbidity in India. Coronary Heart Disease affects 
people in the middle age group, however recent reports suggest that even young 
adults between 30-40 years are affected  with increasing frequency. Congential 
Heart Diseases affects children mainly  in the age group of 0-15 years and 
Rheumatic Heart Disease affects children mainly in the age group of 5-15 years. 
Since the causes of this disease is attributed among others to individual life style 
and food habits the doctors are  creating awareness among the people for 
adopting proper life style and food habits to control this disease.

There are various schemes for which central assistance is provided to the 
State Governments/Institutions. The Schemes are as under : Development of 
Oncology Wing 
This scheme is available only for Government Medical Colleges to fill up the 
geographical gaps in the detection and treatment of cancer in the country. It has 
been observed that there is wide geographical gap in the North and North-Eastern 
States. Financial assistance up to Rs. 2.00 crores can be provided to an Institute 
under the scheme for purchase of listed equipments. This is a one time grant. 
Setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit

for setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit in Government Institutions. This is a one-
time grant.

the Non-Governmental Organisations on the specific recommendations of the 
State Government. This is a one-time grant. 
Assistance for Mammography Unit

for setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit. A Central assistance upto Rs. 30.00 lakhs 
can be provided to those Institutions/Organisations who have the facilities for 
treatment of cancer patients and has well-equipped Radiotherapy Department. 
This is also a one-time grant. 
Voluntary Organisation Scheme

Organisations for undertaking health education and early detection activities in 
cancer on the specific recommenda tions of the State Government. District 
Cancer Control Programme

detection and pain relief measures u nder National Cancer Control Programme 
was initiated during the year 1990-91. In this scheme, financial assistance of 
Rs. 15.00 lakhs is provided to the State Government/UT administration for each 
district selected under the scheme with a provision of Rs. 10.00 lakhs per annum

years, the project is to be taken over by the State Government.

(a) whether Government are aware that many private and public blood 
banks are involved in illegal blood trade;

banks? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) There have been isolated incidences

donation programme, the Government of India have taken a number of steps 
such as media campaign through TV, AIR and newspapers, developing IEC 
material for one-to-one communication, observation of National Voluntary Blood 
Donation day on 1 st October every year, encouraging rational use of blood 
among clinicians and the launching of special campaign to educate masses to 
support voluntary blood donation. Strict vigilance is being maintained by Drugs 
Controllers of all States to ensure that no paid donation takes place and no 
unlicensed blood banks operate.

Reason for back log of cases in Courts 
3750. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH : Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that huge backlog of cases in various courts is partly 
because of large number of vacancies of Judges; 
(b) if so, the steps being taken to fill them and by when these are likely to 
be filled up; and 
(c) whether Government would evolve a permanent machinery to ensure 
that the vacancies of High Court Judges are not held up for want of 
recommendations from the courts concerned ? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
ARUN JAITLEY): (a) Yes, Sir. Pendency of cases in different courts is arising 
from various complex factors. These, inter alia, include large number of 
vacancies of judges, inade quate judge strength, incr eased institution of cases 
on account of awareness of the rights on the part of the citizens, enactment of 
numerous laws, radical change in the pattern of litigation, frequent adjournment 
of cases, rise in population, lawyers' strike etc. 
(b) There is no vacancy in the Supreme Court. The filling up of the 
vacancies in the High Courts is a c ontinuous consultative process among the 
Constitutional authorities. While every effort is made to fill up the existing 
vacancies expeditiously, vacancies do keep on arising on account of retirement, 
resignation or elevation of Judges. 
130 

[27 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Appointment of judicial officers in Subordinate Judiciary are made by the 
State Governments in consultation with their respective High Courts under articles 
233 and 234 of the Constitution. 
State Governments and the High Courts have been addressed periodically 
on the need to fill up all vacant posts, and create more posts where necessary. 
Hence, no time frame can be fixed for filling up the vacancies. 
(c) In accordance with the procedure for appointment of Judges of High 
Courts, the Chief Justice of a High Court is expected to initiate recommendation 
for filling up vacancies in consultation with the collegium of Judges. On the part 
of the Government of India, the Chief Justices of the High Courts are periodically 
requested to initiate proposals for appointment of Judges in respective High 
Courts. 
One of the items on the National Agenda for Governance of the National 
Democratic Alliance is to constitute a National Judicial Commission which will, 
inter alia, recommend judicial appointments in the High Courts and the Supreme 
Court of India. The proposal, however, would require an amendment to the 
Constitution.

Action to prevent cruelty to Animals 
† 3765. DR. A.K. PATEL: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Prayogshlaon mein bejuban janwaron par Krurta kee seema nahin", 
which appeared in Rashtriya Sahara dated 20th March, 2001; and 
(b) if so, the action Government propose to take to prevent the same ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) The Government has constituted a Commitee under sections 14 to 
20 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 with the purpose of 
controlling and supervising experiments performed on animals. The Com-
mittee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals 
has formulated rules governing the procedures for experimentation, which 
have been notified through the Breeding of and Experiments on Animals 
(Control and Supervision) Rules, 1998 and experiments on Animals (Control 
and Supervision) (Amendment) Rules, 200 1. As per rule all the scientific 
institutes/establishments performing experiments/breeding have to register 
themselves with the Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of 
Experiments on Animals. The Committee lays down the guidelines to be 
followed by all establishments for the maintenance of animals and animal 
houses. On application by the institutions and on being satisfied about the 
standards of ethical use of animals, this Committee gives suggestion to the 
institutions. The Committee has also been keeping close watch on the 
condition of the animal houses and the process of experimentation and has 
taken necessary action against several institutions, where violations have 
been reported.

Extension of 73rd and 74th Constitutional (Amendment) Act, 1992 to Hilly 
Scheduled Areas 
3780. SHRI W. ANGOU SINGH: Will the Minister ofTRIBAL AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government are contemplating to extend the 73rd and 74th 
Constitution (Amendment) Act, 1992 to the hilly scheduled areas; 
3815 RSS/2001—11 161 

[27 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the difference between Sixth Schedule and 73rd and 74th Constitution 
Amendment Act, 1992; and 
(c) the recommendations made by the Bhuria Commission regarding the 
extension of these two Acts ? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JUAL ORAM): (a) Yes, Sir. 
The Government has initiated the process of consulting the concerrned State 
Governments, District Autonomous Councils, Autonomous Councils and 
Political Parties in the North-Eastern States for incorporating the provisions of 
the 73rd and 74th Constitution (Amendment) Act, 1992 to the hilly Scheduled 
Areas. 
(b) Under Sixth Schedule, there is a provision of creation of District 
Autonomous Councils and governance as per traditional tribal institutions in 
those areas. The Sixth Schedule focuses on the first tier and does not concern 
itself with tiers below like Block and Village level. The powers and functions are 
laid down in the Sixth Schedule itself. 
73rd and 74th Constitution (Amendment) Acts provide to form three tier 
Panchayati Raj institution in Rural Areas and Local Self Government in Urban 
Areas with power and functions as laid  down in the Panchayati Raj Acts of 
States as extended to Scheduled Areas. It also has provisions of reservation for 
women, SC/ST and Other Backward Classes. The provision of these two Acts 
are not applicable in Nagaland and Sixth Schedule areas of Assam, Meghalaya, 
Mizoram and Tripura- 
(c) A statement showing major recommendations of Bhuria Committee is 
annexed. 
Statement 
Major Recommendations made by the Bhuria Committee 
1. The Constitution 73rd (Amendment) Act, 1992 envisages a 3-tier 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (P.R.Is.) whereas the Committee has 
envisaged 4-tiers. One tier below the Gram Panchayat level which is not 
envisaged in 1992 Act, has been recommended for the Scheduled Areas. 
This has been done to take care of the traditional Village Councils 
which have been performing varied functions-religious, political, 
economic, judicial etc. The Committee recommends that the Gram Sabha 
may nominate its Executive Council or Village Council which may be 
the traditional body and may delegate to it functions like execution of 
162 

RAJYA SABHA [27 August, 2001 ] 
development works. The Committee also recommends the nomination 
of the members not exceeding five in the Autonomous District Councils 
to give representation to minority tribal communities who cannot find 
place in the election process. The nominations are to be made in 
consultation with the Governor. 
2. ( The Committee is of the view that association of the Scheduled Tribe 
Lok Sabha M.Ps, at the intermediate (block) Panchayat and District 
Councils be made. The representation of both Scheduled Tribes and 
non-S.T. MLAs in these two tiers should also be included. 
3. The Committee while recommending functions envisaged under the 
6th Schedule recommends to include subjects that are indicated in the 
11th Schedule of the Constitution as the latter are more wide ranging. 
The powers, functions and procedures proposed for different tiers may 
be seen at Annexures A, B, C & D of the Committee's Report. It may be 
noted that one of the functions given to the Panchayati Raj institutions 
is consideration of requisitions for land acquisition for purposes other 
than defence, railways, roads, e ducation and health institutions and 
approval of schemes of rehabilitation acceptable to the affected persons 
and implementation of the Scheme of rehabilitation and cognizance 
and adjudication of all civil disputes including debts and other liabilities 
and criminal offences not being heinous crimes like murder, dacoity. 
Education and Health sectors have been made the first charge on the 
funds received by the Panchayati Raj institutions. 
4. It is suggested that funds given to the Panchayats including funds 
under first provision to Article 275(1) of the Constitution should be 
placed in the "charged" category to avoid any fear of misutilisation or 
diversion. It is also suggested that funds under TSP may be quantified 
and placed at the disposal of Au tonomous District Council for 
distribution among the Panchayats in the Districts. Moreover to the 
extent possible, the Central and State Governments should devise 
procedures for direct allotment of funds to the Autonomous District 
Councils. 
5. The Committee recommen ds that all Government servants and 
functionaries of institutions concerned with the functions of a 
Panchayat in a Scheduled Areas and located within its jurisdiction will 
be under its control. 
163 

[27 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
6. The Committee further recommends that the remaining Tribal Sub Plan 
areas like MADA areas as well as similar other blocks (referring to 
clusters) should be included in the Scheduled Areas. 
7. It is recommended by the Committee that the Tribes Advisory Council 
and the Autonomous District Council in the Scheduled Areas should 
review the existing laws for their relevance and applicability and take 
action necessary for exclusion of those that are not relevant and 
inclusion of those that are useful. 
8. The Committee also suggests to constitute a Central Advisory Council 
primarily to advise on any disputes between State Government and die 
TAC or between the District Council and TAC. This will, while ensuring 
federal character of the State, will have the merit of resolving the disputes 
at the State level by way of consultation and dialogue between differing 
  bodies closer to the ground reality and the grass roots.

3813. DR. Y. LAKSHMI PRASAD : Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of procedure of dea ling with the complaints received 
regarding subletting of Government quarters and the time taken for decision in 
such cases; 
(b) the details of complaints received through Residents' Welfare 
Associations and from other residents of subletting of quarters of Type-Ill of 
General Pool in Delhi from 1 st July, 2000 to 30th June, 2001; 
(c) the details of complaints received from 1st July, 2000 to 30th June, 
2001 of subletting of quarters allotted from special quotas in Delhi; and 
(d) the details of action taken and the details of cases pending with reasons 
for the delay in taking action? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF UfcBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) Regular inspections are carried out by dedicated teams of 
officers of Directorate of Estates in order to detect subletting in Government 
Quarters. The procedure for dealing with  the cases of suspected subletting is 
provided under the Allotment Rules and guidelines framed thereunder. As per 
prescribed procedure, suspected cases of subletting are dealt with as under : 
(i) A show cause notice is issued to the concerned allottee giving time 
of fifteen days to appear before the Deciding Authority. 
(ii) Once subletting is established, allotment of the quarter is cancelled, 
along with consequential penalties like debarment of the allottee 
from future allotment for the remaining period of service, payment of 
damages for unauthorised stay beyond the date of order of 
cancellation and advising the concerned Department/Ministry to 
initiate disciplinary proceedings against the delinquent official. 
(iii) The allottee has the right of appeal to the Director of Estates within 
30 days of the receipt of the order. 
(iv) On rejection of appeal, the allottee is required to vacate the 
Government quarter forthwith. 
198 

[27 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) In case of non-vacation of the quarter by the allottee, eviction 
proceedings are initiated under th e Public Premises (Eviction of 
Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The proceedings under the 
said Act being quasi-judicial in nature, no time frame may be fixed. 
(b) and (c) A total number of 169 complaints of subletting of quarters of 
Type-Ill of General Pool were received from the Residents Welfare Associations 
and other residents from July, 2000 to June, 2001. However, there are no quarters 
which are earmarked under special quotas. 
(d) There have been 66 cases where subletting of quarters is suspected. 
After following the due process of law, cancellation of allotment has been done 
in 21 cases besides department of allottees from seeking further allotment for the 
remaining period of their service. In addition, the concerned disciplinary 
authorities have also been advised to take disciplinary action against the 
delinquent Government servants under the relevant Conduct Rules. In 13 cases, 
the deciding authority has concluded 'no subletting' and the remaining 32 cases are 
at different stages of hearing before the deciding authority as per Allotment Rules.

The Indian Divorce (Amendment) Bill, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS AND 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): I am extremely grateful 
to you. Mr. Chairman, Sir. I was also permitted, on Thursday afternoon, to 
move the Indian Divorce (Amendment) Bill and to explain as to what this Bill 
was all about. Sir, the Indian Divoice Act, 1869, that was enacted in the last 
century, was almost an exact replica of the English Matrimonial Causes Act of 
1857. Thereafter, there was a great demand for changes and improvements, 
in terms of gender equality, in the Eng lish law, and, in 1923, the English Law 
itself Was changed. In the last 45 ye ars, we have made several attempts to 
improve and change several clauses in this lav/. The Law Commission, on 4 
occasions, i.e., through its I5thReport, the 22nd 
 
 
218 

RAJYA SABHA   [27 August, 2001] 
Report, the 19 Report and the 164 Report, had suggested certain changes to 
the Act itself. Thereafter, several provisio ns of this Act were  also called into 
question before several High Courts in the country, and two particular 
provisions, i.e., Section 10 and Section 17, were held to be ultra vires and 
struck down by several High Courts of the country. I had, therefore, in 
December last year, introduced this Bill , after consultations  with members of 
the community. It has always been a polic y of the Central Government that 
when changes in personal laws are made, we make a concerted effort to have 
large-scale discussions with the community itself, before those changes are 
suggested; and when changes had been suggested by us in December, they 
were suggested essentially to those two provisions which had been struck 
down by the courts. And, in order to fill the vacuum created by the courts' 
striking those grounds and consequent ial changes, those changes were 
introduced. The Bill was then referred to the Standing Committee itself, and 
the Standing Committee had extensive discussions. There were several 
representations made, and a very larg e number of organisations appeared 
before the Standing Committee; they had also separately met me -- the 
Catholic Bishops Conference of India, the National Council of Churches of 
India, the Joint Women Programme, etc. I am glad to say that almost all of 
them not only supported t he initial two suggestions, but also wanted several 
new suggestions and improvements to this Bill to be made. The Standing 
Committee, except one, accepted all th e suggestions which were made. And, 
when the matter came up before the Government, except one suggestion, we 
have also accepted all the suggestions which were made by the community. 
The only one suggestion which we have not accepted relates to empowering 
certain religions authorities to settle certain civil issues relating to marriage 
and dissolution of marriage itself. We could not accept this suggestion 
because, under our scheme of law, as fa r as civil rights are concerned, the 
power and authority to decide them will only be vested in judicial and court 
authority, and that power cannot be abdicated in favour of any other agency. If 
I may, Sir, just explain the changes which have been made as a result of the 
recommendations of the Standing Commi ttee, which I am also proposing 
through the amendments which I have mov ed. Section 7 of the original Act 
says -- because it was an 1869 Act -- "the law laid down in relation to this Act 
by the courts in England will apply." The Supreme Court has already held that 
after 1947, because of our own sovereignty and the sovereign jurisdiction of 
our own courts, the law laid down by another jurisdiction, in another country, 
cannot be compulsorily applicable to our laws.   Therefore, 
219 

[27 August, 2001]   RAJYA SABHA 
Section 7 is proposed to be amended. T he most significant change is made to 
Section 10. Section 10, which had been struck down by about five High Courts 
in the country, gave different grounds  of dissolution of marriage to the 
husband, and entirely different grounds of dissolution of marriage to the wives. 
In fact, the case of the wife was very difficult, because even adultery itself was 
not a ground; something more than adultery has to take place, cruelty with 
adultery or bigamy with adultery was a ground. This had been struck down on 
the grounds of its being ultra vires. We had suggested certain equal grounds 
but, after consultations with the representatives of the community, the 
Standing Committee has suggested a new formulation, where most of the 
common law grounds which are applicable in other laws elsewhere in the 
world and in India are equal grounds now sought to be made available both to 
the wife and the husband. Therefore, the gender bias in Section 10 has been 
corrected. The rights of the wife and husband are both the same. 
There was another discomfort which was caused to the community, 
by the provisions of Section 17. After evidence was recorded by various district 
courts, the confirmation of the decree of dissolution had to be made by the 
High Court, and in the High Court, the matter used to go to a full Bench. 
Therefore, not only the time consum ed was very large, besides time, 
consumption it was also a costly exerci se. This provision had also been struck 
down by a High Court, and, therefore, now, this provision is sought to be 
deleted altogether. There are several other  provisions; for instance. Provision 
enabling the husband, in the event of an allegation of adultery against the wife, 
to start claiming damages from the adulterer who is living with her; 
compensation in relation to Section 35 in  relation to cost to be claimed in the 
event of adultery; cases where the proper ty of the wife would be taken away 
and vested either in the husband or in  the children, in case one of the 
matrimonial offences was proved. Thes e are all one-sided provisions since 
corresponding rights have not been given to the wife. The Standing Committee 
felt that all these provisions were now required to be deleted. This unanimous 
report of the Standing Committee, as I said, has been accepted by the 
Government. With all these amendments, while removing the provisions that 
created a bias, one very important clause  has been changed. About this the 
Members of the House had commented in  relation to other discussions. The 
outer limit of maintenance for a Christia n wife was one-fifth of the husband's 
income. The Standing Committee felt that this capping was no longer 
necessary and it was for the judicial aut hority to decide looking to the merit of 
the case.  We have accepted that 
220 

RAJYA SABHA   [27 August, 2001] 
entire recommendation. The members of the community who met us, also 
felt that even though the title is Divor ce Act, yet, since there are segments 
in the Christian community who do not appreciate the use of that word, in 
the text of the Act itself, the word used should be 'dissolution of marriage' 
itself. We have respected that sent iment and, therefore, have used that 
word. ^  
Section 10A again has been suggested by the community to be 
added as a provision for dissolution of the marriage by mutual consent. This 
provision was necessary, because.in a case, where the marriage does not 
work, it was still necessary for one party to make serious allegations against 
the other, prove those allegations and then only the marriage could be 
dissolved. The community felt that this was no longer necessary. When both 
parties are willing, it could be dissolved by mutual consent. We have also 
accepted that suggestion recommended by the Standing Committee. 
Sir, i commend to the House that this Bill be passed.

THE GOVERNMENT OF UNION TERRITORIES AND 
THE GOVERNMENT OF NATIONAL CAPITAL TERRITORY 
OF DELHI (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2001 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): Sir, I move:- 
"That the Bill further to amend the Government of      Union 
Territories Act,  1963 and  the Government     of  National  
Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991,   as passed by the Lok 
Sabha, be taken into   consideration". 
It is a very simple Bill, Sir. Both  the Union Territories, the National 
Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Pondicherry, have 
separate legislatures. They have their Consolidated Fund also. But both the 
legislatures do not have the power to  borrow from the market upon the 
Consolidated Funds of their respective Union Territories. Secondly, provisions 
are being provided here to have public account. They do not have any public 
account. Provisions are being made by virtue of this amendment to enable 
them to have separate public accounts. 
Sir, the Bill seeks to amend the Government of Union Territories 
Act, 1963 in relation to Pondicherry, and the Government of National Capital 
Territory of Delhi Act, 1991 in relation to the National Capital Territory of 
Delhi, to provide for giving the two Union Territories having legislative 
assemblies the power and authority to borrow from market and to give 
guarantees upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of the Union 
Territory concerned.   The reason is that  the two Union Territories have their 
own Consolidated Funds but they do not have the power to borrow from the 
market. The Lt. Governors of these two Union Territories would also be 
allowed to exercise the powers of the Government of India in this regard. In 
addition, provisions are being made for having their separate public accounts 
as well as their own cash balances with the Reserve Bank of India. This 
revised arrangement is envisaged to ena ble the Reserve Bank of India to 
monitor the ways and means position of  these two Union Territories on a day-
to-day basis, and bring them within the normal discipline relating to the 
limitations and r egulations of overdraft, which is already applicable in respect 
of the State Governments. This will also enable the two Union Territories to 
operate their finances on their own, in real terms, and encourage them to 
observe strict financial discipline. With these words, Sir, I commend this Bill to 
this august House for approval.

SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN (Karnataka): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, thank 
you for giving me this opportunity to speak on the Short Duration Discussion. 
Today, we are discussing the Report of the Group of Ministers on the National 
Security. My other colleagues, here, have spoken on various aspects of the 
national security and also on the Report. I would like to confine myself to a few 
paragraphs of the Report which deal with  a statement. It says, "That a recent 
phenomenon is the mushrooming of the pan-Islamic militant outfits with links 
with radical organisations in Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Sudan and in some other 
West Asian countries funded by Saudi Arabia and Gulf sources.    Many new 
Madarasas have come up all

Madarasas. The Madarasas are the religi ous institutions. We are a secular 
country. Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution gives us the religious freedom

formation of Pakistan or the ISI activiti es have started. Sir, Madarasas are

years ago from a Madarsa. Today, there is an attempt to tarnish the image of

nobody to defend them. But, only to say that the Madarasas are involved in

through a systematic campaign against the Madarasas that these Madarasas 
are anti-Indian, is not good. Sir, even the highly educated people are forced to 
think whether these Madarasas are really involving in such activities. What are 
the things Madarasas taught? If you hav e any instances, prove it. Show it. 
Last year, the hon. Home Minister also  said the same thing. When he was 
asked, 'Whether you have any proof of the activity?', he said, 'No.' In 1994, the 
Home Ministry said that there was no proof of ISI activities in the madarsas. 
So, this is a very important thing. What they say is, it is not a threat to the 
country's communal harmony. Sir, here, I would like to point out that the 
Bajrang Dal has begun a major exercise in training its members in arms in 
Lucknow. According to the Bajrang Dal Members, their goal is to train young 
college students in the use of firearms  so that they can protect the Dai's 
philosophy of hindutva. A guesthouse in Lucknow has been converted into a 
training centre. The students who are barely 20 years old are undergoing 
training in shooting and martial acts. The Bajrang Dal says, "When the time 
comes, they will be used as kar sevaks to build the temple at Ayodhaya.' This 
has been stated by the Convenor of Bajrang Dal, Mr. so and so. He said, 
"Through the ISI and other missionaries,  an attempt has been made to bring 
about instability. We are trying to meet th at challenge."   Now,   here is an 
organization which openly says, "We are

Last Friday, while discussing a Private Member's Resolution we were talking

Ministers has made so many recommendations regarding giving more powers

Ministers, consultations should be held and a national consensus should be

to know from a Press report that even the law and order situation in the States

SHRI SURESH A. KESWANI: Sir, I would like to start my 
presentation with an observation on the statement made by one of the 
speakers here that 'we justif y the crisis on the ground that this by itself would 
create its own solution and this by itself would bring new opportunities and 
from that the nation would rise'. Sir, this is a very strange way of dealing with a 
very serious situation we are talk ing about. One does hope that the 
Government would find that kind of a solution which our friend was dreaming 
about and would overcome this crisis wh ich is eating into the vitals of the 
country. Let us examine what has happen ed in the last three years. In 1998. 
when this Government came to power, without any significant preparations, 
without fully comprehending the consequences, they went in for Pokhran-2. 
What were the considerations? Was t he consideration nation building? Was 
the consideration long-term thinking as to  what kind of role this nation must 
play in the comity of nations? Was it  any well-thought out strategy? We found 
very important leaders issuing threats to our Western neighbours. We found a 
senior leader, a former Defence Minister, naming our Northern most-powerful 
neighbour as our enemy number one. I do not know what kind of defence 
strategy, what kind of foreign affairs strategy and what kind of economic 
strategy they had in mind. The first consequence was, sanctions were 
imposed on the country and the country found itself unequal to the problems 
which directly resulted from those sanctions. 
We shout from the housetops that we  don't care for sanctions that, 
actually, it is the people who would not be able to give us the aid are 
greater sufferers than we, and that we can do without it. And, what 
happened as a result? We found a series of things happening thereafter, 
resulting in the losing of our control on the economy. And we find that the 
Government was indulging more in politics than in nation-building activities. 
Every measure, every announcement, was with some kind of an ulterior 
motive, of getting some electoral benefits  here or some polit ical benefitthere, 
and the national interest was completely forgotten.    Sir, we had a situation 
where intelligence failure took plac e. We had a situation where we had 
another gimmick called the Lahore Yatra; we had a great failure there. We 
found that we were simply in a situat ion which was nothing less than a Faux 
Pas. We had the Kargil War on hand; we had the Government losing vote of 
confidence; we had a situation where this Government was making use of 
those six months, virtually* indulging as  though they got a licence, and did so 
many things which no well-thinking Government could have possibly done with 
Parliament being present.   We found the political power

[27 August, 2001]   RAJYA SABHA 
being used for motives other than building of the nation. Slowly and slowly, our 
economy started suffering as a result. We had the re-election of this 
Government with the support of so  many State Governments. The new 
Government, which came in place, announces another economic policy, goes 
to the housetop and makes all kinds of declarations, again with political ends 
in mind, and not with any long-term thinking, not with any long-term 
programme, not with any long-term strategy, not knowing how to use their 
scarce resources; and, as a result of these, we found the markets going one 
way and the Government going the other way round. We found the 
Government losing control on every sector. We found scams taking place in 
every field. We found all kinds of allegations being made against the 
Government; we found the confidence of the public going down in our financial 
system, in our banking system, in our Unit Trust; we find chaos everywhere. 
What is .the reason for this? Is it not a fact that they all have been indulging 
more in politics? We have created a situation where we have a respected 
Prime Minister, - he is also a poet - but  a very weak Centre; we have State 
Governments and State parties virtually ruling the roost -- a situation like the 
Bahadur Shah Zafar's rule in those times. He was a wonderful man -- he too 
was a poet -- but it was the States whic h were virtually ruling the roost. Where 
are we going from here? How are we going to overcome the situation? In the 
Report, they are asking for more powers. How are these powers going to be 
used? Will they be able to use these powers to overcome this situation? 
Nobody can deny the fact that we need to strengthen the Union Government. 
Unless we have the strength, these problems cannot be overcome - 
communal strife, internal problems, States fighting amongst themselves; 
community clashes, ISI having connections with LTTE and with the Naga 
outfits. We have also seen something happening in Nepal. All these are 
nothing but the symptoms of one malaise which is afflicting this nation. It is 
that this nation is perceived as a very weak nation. How do you give strength? 
I think time has come when we all have to apply our minds and find out ways 
to strengthen the Union Government. One of the ways that we could consider 
is that our Prime Minister should be elected by Parliament for a term of five 
years - just as we elect the Vice-President - whom we can impeach if we find 
something wrong with him. Once he is el ected for a period of five years, at 
least, we can have a Government which will remain in office for five years. 
What could be the possible consequences of this? How do we make sure that 
it becomes foolproof? How do we do various other things whereby this 
Government becomes responsible and responsive?   These are
